c05-p01: Every day I learned something about the planet, about the departure, about the journey. It came very gently, by chance, as thoughts came up. That is how, on the third day, I learned of the drama of the baobabs.
c05-p02: This time again it was thanks to the sheep, for all of a sudden the little prince asked me, as if seized by a grave doubt:
c05-p03: "It is true, isn't it, that sheep eat little bushes?"
c05-p06: I did not understand why it was so important that sheep should eat little bushes. But the little prince added:
c05-p08: I pointed out to the little prince that baobabs are not little bushes, but trees as big as churches, and that even if he took a whole herd of elephants home with him, the herd would not get the better of a single baobab.
c05-p09: The idea of the herd of elephants made the little prince laugh:
c05-p10: "We would have to put them one on top of the other..."
c05-p12: "Baobabs, before they grow big, start out by being little."
c05-p13: "That's right! But why do you want your sheep to eat the little baobabs?"
c05-p14: He answered me: "Oh, come on! You know!" as if it were perfectly obvious. And it took a great effort of thought on my part to work out the problem all by myself.
c05-p15: And indeed, on the little prince's planet, as on every planet, there were good plants and bad plants. And so there were good seeds from good plants and bad seeds from bad plants. But seeds are invisible. They sleep in the secret depths of the earth until one of them takes it into its head to wake up. Then it stretches, and at first it pushes timidly towards the sun a lovely little harmless sprig. If it is the sprig of a radish or a rose bush, you can let it grow however it likes. But if it is a bad plant, you must pull the plant out at once, as soon as you have recognised it. Now there were some terrible seeds on the little prince's planet... they were the seeds of baobabs. The soil of the planet was infested with them. And a baobab, if you get to it too late, you can never get rid of. It takes over the whole planet. It bores right through it with its roots. And if the planet is too small, and if the baobabs are too many, they make it burst into pieces.
c05-p16: "It is a question of discipline," the little prince told me later on. "When you have finished washing and dressing in the morning, you must carefully wash and dress the planet. You must make yourself pull up the baobabs regularly, as soon as you can tell them apart from the rose bushes, which they look very much like when they are very young. It is very tedious work, but very easy."
c05-p17: And one day he advised me to work hard at making a beautiful drawing, so as to get this well into the heads of the children where I come from. "If they ever travel," he said to me, "it may be useful to them. Sometimes there is no harm in putting off a piece of work until later. But when it comes to baobabs, it is always a catastrophe. I knew a planet that was lived on by a lazy man. He had neglected three little bushes..."
c05-p18: And so, following the little prince's directions, I drew that planet. I do not much like taking the tone of a moralist. But the danger of baobabs is so little known, and the risks run by anyone who might lose his way on an asteroid are so considerable, that for once I am making an exception to my reserve. I say: "Children! Watch out for the baobabs!" It is to warn my friends of a danger they had been brushing past for a long time, as I had myself, without knowing it, that I worked so hard on this drawing. The lesson I was passing on was worth the trouble. Perhaps you will ask: Why is there no other drawing in this book as magnificent as the drawing of the baobabs? The answer is very simple: I tried, but I could not manage it. When I drew the baobabs I was carried along by a feeling of urgency.
c06-p01: Ah, little prince! Little by little, in this way, I came to understand your small, melancholy life. For a long time your only entertainment had been the sweetness of the sunsets. I learned that new detail on the morning of the fourth day, when you said to me:
c06-p02: "I am very fond of sunsets. Let us go and look at a sunset..."
c06-p06: At first you looked very surprised, and then you laughed at yourself. And you said to me:
c06-p07: "I keep thinking I am at home!"
c06-p08: Just so. When it is noon in the United States, the sun, as everyone knows, is setting over France. If you could get to France in one minute, you could watch the sunset. Unfortunately France is much too far away. But on your tiny planet, all you had to do was move your chair a few steps. And you would watch the twilight whenever you wished...
c06-p09: "One day, I saw the sun set forty-four times!"
c06-p10: And a little later you added:
c06-p11: "You know... when you are so very sad, you love sunsets..."
c06-p12: "Were you so very sad, then, on the day of the forty-four times?" But the little prince did not answer.
c07-p01: On the fifth day, again thanks to the sheep, this secret of the little prince's life was revealed to me. He asked me abruptly, without any preamble, as though it were the fruit of a problem he had long been turning over in silence:
c07-p02: "A sheep, if it eats little bushes, does it eat flowers too?"
c07-p03: "A sheep eats everything it comes across."
c07-p06: "Then the thorns, what are they for?"
c07-p07: I did not know. At that moment I was very busy trying to unscrew a bolt in my engine that was screwed in too tight. I was very worried, for my breakdown was beginning to look very serious to me, and the drinking water running out made me fear the worst.
c07-p09: The little prince never let go of a question once he had asked it. I was irritated by my bolt, and I answered with the first thing that came into my head:
c07-p10: "Thorns are no use at all. They are pure spite on the flowers' part!"
c07-p12: But after a silence he flung at me, with a kind of resentment:
c07-p13: "I don't believe you! Flowers are weak. They are naive. They reassure themselves as best they can. They think they are terrible with their thorns..."
c07-p14: I made no answer. At that moment I was saying to myself: "If this bolt still won't give, I'll knock it out with a hammer." The little prince broke into my thoughts again:
c07-p15: "And you, you really think that flowers..."
c07-p16: "No! No! I don't think anything! I just said whatever came into my head. I am busy with serious matters!"
c07-p19: He saw me there, hammer in hand, my fingers black with engine grease, bending over an object that seemed to him very ugly.
c07-p21: That made me a little ashamed. But he went on, without mercy:
c07-p22: "You mix everything up... you jumble it all together!"
c07-p23: He was truly very angry. He tossed his golden hair in the wind:
c07-p24: "I know a planet where there is a crimson-faced gentleman. He has never smelled a flower. He has never looked at a star. He has never loved anyone. He has never done anything but add up figures. And all day long he says over and over, just like you: 'I am a serious man! I am a serious man!' and it makes him swell up with pride. But he is not a man, he is a mushroom!"
c07-p27: The little prince had now gone quite pale with anger.
c07-p28: "For millions of years flowers have been making thorns. For millions of years sheep have been eating flowers all the same. And it isn't serious to try to understand why they go to so much trouble to make themselves thorns that are never any use? It isn't important, the war between the sheep and the flowers? It isn't more serious and more important than the sums of a fat red gentleman? And if I know, myself, a flower that is unique in the world, that exists nowhere except on my planet, and that a little sheep can wipe out in a single bite, just like that, one morning, without even realising what he is doing, that isn't important!"
c07-p29: He flushed red, then went on:
c07-p30: "If someone loves a flower of which there is only one in all the millions and millions of stars, that is enough to make him happy when he looks at them. He says to himself: 'My flower is out there somewhere...' But if the sheep eats the flower, for him it is as if, all of a sudden, every star went out! And that isn't important!"
c07-p31: He could say nothing more. All at once he burst into sobs. Night had fallen. I had let my tools drop. What did I care about my hammer, my bolt, thirst, or death? There was, on a star, on a planet, on mine, the Earth, a little prince to be comforted! I took him in my arms. I rocked him. I said to him: "The flower you love is not in danger... I will draw a muzzle for your sheep... I will draw you some armour for your flower... I..." I did not really know what to say. I felt very clumsy. I did not know how to reach him, where to find him... It is such a mysterious place, the land of tears!
c08-p01: I soon learned to know this flower better. On the little prince's planet there had always been very simple flowers, adorned with a single ring of petals, which took up no room at all and bothered no one. They would appear one morning in the grass, and then fade away in the evening. But this one had sprouted one day from a seed blown in from no one knows where, and the little prince had watched very closely over this sprig, which did not look like the other sprigs. It might have been a new kind of baobab. But the little bush soon stopped growing and began to get a flower ready. The little prince, who was present at the appearance of an enormous bud, felt sure that some miraculous vision would come out of it; but the flower would not stop getting ready to be beautiful, sheltered in her green chamber. She chose her colours with care. She dressed herself slowly, she adjusted her petals one by one. She did not want to come out all crumpled like the poppies. She wanted to appear only in the full radiance of her beauty. Oh, yes! She was very vain! Her mysterious adorning had gone on, then, for days and days. And then one morning, exactly at the hour of sunrise, she showed herself.
c08-p02: And she, who had worked with such great precision, said with a yawn:
c08-p03: "Ah! I am hardly awake... I beg your pardon... My hair is still all in a mess..."
c08-p04: The little prince, then, could not hold back his admiration:
c08-p06: "Am I not?" the flower answered sweetly. "And I was born at the same moment as the sun..."
c08-p07: The little prince guessed easily enough that she was not too modest, but she was so moving!
c08-p08: "It is time for breakfast, I believe," she soon added. "Would you be so kind as to think of me..."
c08-p09: And the little prince, quite abashed, went and fetched a watering can of fresh water, and served the flower.
c08-p10: So she had very quickly begun to torment him with her rather touchy vanity. One day, for instance, speaking of her four thorns, she had said to the little prince:
c08-p11: "Let the tigers come, with their claws!"
c08-p12: "There are no tigers on my planet," the little prince had objected, "and besides, tigers do not eat grass."
c08-p13: "I am not a grass," the flower had sweetly replied.
c08-p15: "I am not at all afraid of tigers, but I have a horror of draughts. You wouldn't have a screen?"
c08-p16: "A horror of draughts... that is bad luck, for a plant," the little prince had remarked. "This flower is very complicated..."
c08-p17: "In the evening you will put me under a glass globe. It is very cold where you live. It is badly arranged. Where I come from..."
c08-p18: But she had broken off. She had come in the form of a seed. She could not have known anything of other worlds. Humiliated at having let herself be caught preparing so naive a lie, she had coughed two or three times, to put the little prince in the wrong:
c08-p20: "I was going to fetch it, but you were talking to me!"
c08-p21: Then she had forced her cough, so that he would suffer remorse all the same.
c08-p22: And so the little prince, in spite of all the good will of his love, had soon come to doubt her. He had taken words of no importance seriously, and he had become very unhappy.
c08-p23: "I ought not to have listened to her," he confided to me one day. "One must never listen to flowers. One must look at them and breathe their fragrance. Mine filled my planet with perfume, but I did not know how to take delight in it. That business about the claws, which had annoyed me so much, ought to have filled me with tenderness..."
c08-p25: "I did not know how to understand anything, then! I should have judged her by what she did and not by what she said. She filled my world with fragrance and with light. I should never have run away! I should have guessed the tenderness behind her poor little tricks. Flowers are so contradictory! But I was too young to know how to love her."
c09-p01: I believe that for his escape he took advantage of a migration of wild birds. On the morning of his departure he put his planet in good order. He carefully swept out his active volcanoes. He owned two active volcanoes. And they were very handy for heating his breakfast in the morning. He also owned one volcano that was extinct. But, as he said, "One never knows!" So he swept out the extinct volcano as well. If they are well swept out, volcanoes burn gently and steadily, without any eruptions. Volcanic eruptions are like fires in a chimney. Of course, on our Earth we are much too small to sweep out our volcanoes. That is why they bring us so much trouble.
c09-p02: The little prince also pulled up, with a little melancholy, the last shoots of the baobabs. He believed he would never be coming back. But all these familiar tasks seemed to him, that morning, extremely sweet. And when he watered the flower for the last time, and got ready to shelter her under her glass globe, he found that he wanted to cry.
c09-p04: But she did not answer him.
c09-p06: The flower coughed. But it was not because of her cold.
c09-p07: "I have been silly," she said to him at last. "I ask your forgiveness. Try to be happy."
c09-p08: He was surprised that there were no reproaches. He stood there quite bewildered, the glass globe held up in the air. He did not understand this quiet sweetness.
c09-p09: "Yes, of course I love you," the flower said to him. "You never knew it, and that was my fault. It does not matter at all. But you have been just as silly as I. Try to be happy... Leave that globe alone. I don't want it any more."
c09-p11: "My cold is not as bad as all that... The cool night air will do me good. I am a flower."
c09-p13: "I must put up with two or three caterpillars if I want to get to know the butterflies. They say it is so very beautiful. Otherwise, who will come to visit me? You will be far away. As for the big animals, I am not afraid of anything. I have my claws."
c09-p14: And she innocently showed her four thorns. Then she added:
c09-p15: "Don't linger like that, it is tiresome. You have decided to go away. Now go."
c09-p16: For she did not want him to see her crying. She was such a proud flower...
